newsitem.title: HONG KONG: APT Sat shares seen in weak debut on risk fears.
newsitem.headline: APT Sat shares seen in weak debut on risk fears.

text.p: Technical risks linked to APT Satellite Holdings Ltd's business have kept investors away from the satellite service firm's IPO, and its shares now look set for a weak market debut on Wednesday, analysts said.
The China-backed company said on Tuesday that its initial public offering (IPO) in Hong Kong of 9.45 million shares had been only 65.5 percent subscribed.
The price was set at HK$13.40 per share, below an indicative range of HK$15.31 to HK$17.71.
Of the 105 million shares offered globally, APT said the 94.5 million shares offered to U.S. and international investors were moderately oversubscribed.
Shares offered to employees were 27.9 percent subscribed.

"The relatively poor subscription response has reflected investors' concerns over its earnings prospects, especially since there are many underlying uncertainties which will affect its earnings," said one analyst at a regional brokerage.

Risks associated with the launch of satellites -- namely launch or in-orbit failures -- would affect the company's present and future satellites and have an adverse impact on the company's operations and financial condition, analysts said.
APT launched its first satellite, APSTAR I, in July 1994 but the launch of APSTAR II in January 1995 failed.
It launched APSTAR IA in July 1996 and plans to launch APSTAR IIR in mid-1997 on a Chinese Long March 3B rocket.
A Long March 3B rocket carrying an Intelsat satellite exploded and crashed in February.
APT said in its listing prospectus that the launch failure might result in higher insurance premiums for the company for the launch and initial in-orbit insurance on APSTAR IIR.

The company said in its listing prospectus it was seeking bids for the launch and initial in-orbit insurance for APSTAR IIR and there could be no assurance that it would obtain future insurance on satisfactory terms.

In-orbit insurance would only cover the book value and not the replacement cost of a satellite. Insurance coverage does not compensate APT for the interruption of its business and similar losses, the company said in its prospectus.
"Its earnings would be considered more secure if it successfully launches its satellite," said Michael Ng, analyst at ASG Investment.

Analysts said local investors were also unfamiliar with the satellite business, and the weak performance of APT's rival Asia Satellite Telecommunications Holdings Ltd (AsiaSat) since its June 1996 listing would also discourage investors.
AsiaSat shares debuted strongly but have sagged since, ending on Tuesday at HK$18.00, below their issue price of HK$20.00 per share.

APT currently serves the satellite communications market in Asia with special emphasis on China. Its competitors include government-owned and privately-owned international, regional and domestic satellite companies.

The company is controlled by China's Commission of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defence, the Chinese Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, China Aerospace Corp and China Telecommunications Broadcast Satellite Corp.
The company said it expects consolidated profit after taxation but before extraordinary items of not less than HK$74.9 million for the year ending December 1996.

It said about US$149.2 million of the IPO proceeds would be used to repay the principal amount outstanding under an APSTAR IA/IIR loan agreement, and US$61.8 million would be used to fund the construction and launch of APSTAR IIR and for financing future satellite projects.
